claim: In bacteria various tactic responses are mediated by the same cellular pathway.
source: In bacteria various tactic responses are mediated by the same cellular pathway, but sensing of physical stimuli remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial taxis that is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Sensing of physical stimuli in bacteria remains poorly understood.
source: In bacteria various tactic responses are mediated by the same cellular pathway, but sensing of physical stimuli remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In the absence of chemical attractants E. coli exhibits a steady thermophilic response.
source: We show that in the absence of chemical attractants E. coli exhibits a steady thermophilic response, the magnitude of which decreases at higher temperatures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FRET and microfluidics assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The magnitude of the thermophilic response decreases at higher temperatures.
source: We show that in the absence of chemical attractants E. coli exhibits a steady thermophilic response, the magnitude of which decreases at higher temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1C.

claim: Adaptation of wild-type cells to high levels of chemoattractants sensed by only one of the major chemoreceptors leads to inversion of the thermotactic response at intermediate temperatures.
source: Adaptation of wild-type cells to high levels of chemoattractants sensed by only one of the major chemoreceptors leads to inversion of the thermotactic response at intermediate temperatures and bidirectional cell accumulation in a thermal gradient.
evidence: This is supported by FRET and microfluidics data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Adaptation to high levels of chemoattractants sensed by only one major chemoreceptor leads to bidirectional cell accumulation in a thermal gradient.
source: Adaptation of wild-type cells to high levels of chemoattractants sensed by only one of the major chemoreceptors leads to inversion of the thermotactic response at intermediate temperatures and bidirectional cell accumulation in a thermal gradient.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microfluidics experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A mathematical model can explain the bidirectional thermotaxis behavior based on the saturation-dependent kinetics of adaptive receptor methylation.
source: A mathematical model can explain this behavior based on the saturation-dependent kinetics of adaptive receptor methylation.
evidence: This is supported by the mathematical modeling presented in Figure 4 and the Materials and methods section.

claim: The preferred accumulation temperature corresponds to optimal growth in the presence of the chemoattractant serine.
source: Lastly, we find that the preferred accumulation temperature corresponds to optimal growth in the presence of the chemoattractant serine, pointing to a physiological relevance of the observed thermotactic behavior.
evidence: This is supported by growth experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Temperature is one of the crucial environmental factors that determine growth and fitness for many organisms.
source: For many organisms temperature is one of the crucial environmental factors that determine growth and fitness.
evidence: This is general biological knowledge.

claim: Organisms developed sophisticated systems for sensing and responding to temperature.
source: Thus, it is not surprising that organisms developed sophisticated systems for sensing and responding to temperature (Sengupta and Garrity, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The capability to detect and follow environmental temperature gradients (thermotaxis) is inherent to many organisms, from animals to bacteria.
source: Indeed, the capability to detect and follow environmental temperature gradients – thermotaxis – is inherent to many organisms, from animals to bacteria.
evidence: This is general knowledge about thermotaxis across organisms.

claim: In eukaryotes temperature is usually sensed by specific thermal sensors.
source: Although in eukaryotes temperature is usually sensed by specific thermal sensors, behavioral controls by temperature and chemical stimuli are tightly intertwined in the well-studied examples of Caenorhabditis elegans (Kimata et al., 2012) and Drosophila melanogaster (Montell, 2013; Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Behavioral controls by temperature and chemical stimuli are tightly intertwined in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Although in eukaryotes temperature is usually sensed by specific thermal sensors, behavioral controls by temperature and chemical stimuli are tightly intertwined in the well-studied examples of Caenorhabditis elegans (Kimata et al., 2012) and Drosophila melanogaster (Montell, 2013; Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kimata et al., 2012.

claim: Behavioral controls by temperature and chemical stimuli are tightly intertwined in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Although in eukaryotes temperature is usually sensed by specific thermal sensors, behavioral controls by temperature and chemical stimuli are tightly intertwined in the well-studied examples of Caenorhabditis elegans (Kimata et al., 2012) and Drosophila melanogaster (Montell, 2013; Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Montell, 2013 and Ni et al., 2013.

claim: Integration of behavioral responses is even more pronounced in bacteria.
source: Such integration of behavioral responses is even more pronounced in bacteria.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on knowledge of bacterial systems.

claim: In Escherichia coli the thermotactic and chemotactic responses are mediated by the same pathway.
source: In Escherichia coli the thermotactic and chemotactic responses are mediated by the same pathway (Maeda and Imae, 1979; Maeda et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maeda and Imae, 1979 and Maeda et al., 1976.

claim: The tactic behavior of E. coli relies on the control of flagellar motors by a signaling pathway that decreases the rate of tumbles upon an increase in the levels of attractants or upon a decrease in the levels of repellents.
source: The tactic behavior of E. coli generally relies on the control of flagellar motors by a signaling pathway that decreases the rate of 'tumbles' (reorientations) upon an increase in the levels of attractants or upon a decrease in the levels of repellents.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli chemotaxis.

claim: E. coli cells make longer runs in the preferred direction, resulting in a net propagation up attractant gradients.
source: As a result cells make longer runs in the preferred direction, resulting in a net propagation up attractant gradients (Brown and Berg, 1974; Macnab and Koshland, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown and Berg, 1974 and Macnab and Koshland, 1972.

claim: Stimulus recognition in E. coli relies on signaling complexes that consist of transmembrane receptors, the scaffold protein CheW, and the histidine kinase CheA.
source: Stimulus recognition relies on signaling complexes that consist of transmembrane receptors, the scaffold protein CheW, and the histidine kinase CheA (Gegner et al., 1992; Hazelbauer et al., 2008; Sourjik, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gegner et al., 1992; Hazelbauer et al., 2008; and Sourjik, 2004.

claim: Conformational changes induced by binding of chemical ligands in the periplasm are transmitted to the cytoplasmic part of the receptor and control the activity of CheA.
source: Conformational changes that are induced by binding of chemical ligands in the periplasm are transmitted to the cytoplasmic part of the receptor and control the activity of CheA, which is inhibited by attractants and stimulated by repellents (Falke and Hazelbauer, 2001; Hazelbauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Falke and Hazelbauer, 2001 and Hazelbauer et al., 2008.

claim: CheA is inhibited by attractants and stimulated by repellents.
source: Conformational changes that are induced by binding of chemical ligands in the periplasm are transmitted to the cytoplasmic part of the receptor and control the activity of CheA, which is inhibited by attractants and stimulated by repellents (Falke and Hazelbauer, 2001; Hazelbauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Falke and Hazelbauer, 2001 and Hazelbauer et al., 2008.

claim: CheA-mediated phosphorylation of CheY stimulates its binding to the flagellar motor and induces tumbling.
source: CheA-mediated phosphorylation of the response regulator CheY stimulates its binding to the flagellar motor and induces tumbling, whereas dephosphorylation of CheY by the phosphatase CheZ promotes smooth swimming.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the E. coli chemotaxis pathway.

claim: Dephosphorylation of CheY by the phosphatase CheZ promotes smooth swimming.
source: CheA-mediated phosphorylation of the response regulator CheY stimulates its binding to the flagellar motor and induces tumbling, whereas dephosphorylation of CheY by the phosphatase CheZ promotes smooth swimming.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the E. coli chemotaxis pathway.

claim: Adaptation to persistent stimuli in the chemotaxis system is mediated by the methyltransferase CheR and the methylesterase CheB.
source: Adaptation to persistent stimuli in the chemotaxis system is mediated by the methyltransferase CheR and the methylesterase CheB, which adjust the level of receptor methylation and thereby receptor activity dependent on the background stimulation (Goy et al., 1977; Springer et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goy et al., 1977 and Springer et al., 1979.

claim: The chemotaxis system functions as an integral negative feedback circuit.
source: The system functions as an integral negative feedback circuit, whereby CheR preferentially methylates inactive receptors, thus increasing their activity, whereas CheB preferentially demethylates active receptors (Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Shapiro et al., 1995; Terwilliger et al., 1986; Yi et al, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Shapiro et al., 1995; Terwilliger et al., 1986; and Yi et al, 2000.

claim: CheR preferentially methylates inactive receptors, thus increasing their activity.
source: The system functions as an integral negative feedback circuit, whereby CheR preferentially methylates inactive receptors, thus increasing their activity, whereas CheB preferentially demethylates active receptors (Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Shapiro et al., 1995; Terwilliger et al., 1986; Yi et al, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Shapiro et al., 1995; Terwilliger et al., 1986; and Yi et al, 2000.

claim: CheB preferentially demethylates active receptors.
source: The system functions as an integral negative feedback circuit, whereby CheR preferentially methylates inactive receptors, thus increasing their activity, whereas CheB preferentially demethylates active receptors (Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Shapiro et al., 1995; Terwilliger et al., 1986; Yi et al, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Shapiro et al., 1995; Terwilliger et al., 1986; and Yi et al, 2000.

claim: The most abundant receptors in E. coli are Tsr and Tar.
source: The most abundant receptors in E. coli are Tsr and Tar, which respectively sense the amino acids serine and aspartate but can also detect other stimuli (Adler et al., 1973; Greer-Phillips et al., 2003; Kondoh et al., 1979; Maeda et al., 1976; Mesibov and Adler, 1972; Slonczewski et al., 1982; Springer et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Tsr senses the amino acid serine.
source: The most abundant receptors in E. coli are Tsr and Tar, which respectively sense the amino acids serine and aspartate but can also detect other stimuli (Adler et al., 1973; Greer-Phillips et al., 2003; Kondoh et al., 1979; Maeda et al., 1976; Mesibov and Adler, 1972; Slonczewski et al., 1982; Springer et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Tar senses the amino acid aspartate.
source: The most abundant receptors in E. coli are Tsr and Tar, which respectively sense the amino acids serine and aspartate but can also detect other stimuli (Adler et al., 1973; Greer-Phillips et al., 2003; Kondoh et al., 1979; Maeda et al., 1976; Mesibov and Adler, 1972; Slonczewski et al., 1982; Springer et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Tsr and Tar can also detect other stimuli besides serine and aspartate.
source: The most abundant receptors in E. coli are Tsr and Tar, which respectively sense the amino acids serine and aspartate but can also detect other stimuli (Adler et al., 1973; Greer-Phillips et al., 2003; Kondoh et al., 1979; Maeda et al., 1976; Mesibov and Adler, 1972; Slonczewski et al., 1982; Springer et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: All chemoreceptors in E. coli form large mixed clusters in the inner membrane.
source: In the cell, all chemoreceptors form large mixed clusters in the inner membrane, where cooperative interactions between multiple receptors serve to amplify chemotactic stimuli (Ames et al., 2002; Briegel et al., 2012; Sourjik and Berg, 2004; Studdert and Parkinson, 2004; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ames et al., 2002; Briegel et al., 2012; Sourjik and Berg, 2004; Studdert and Parkinson, 2004; and Zhang et al., 2007.

claim: Cooperative interactions between multiple receptors serve to amplify chemotactic stimuli.
source: In the cell, all chemoreceptors form large mixed clusters in the inner membrane, where cooperative interactions between multiple receptors serve to amplify chemotactic stimuli (Ames et al., 2002; Briegel et al., 2012; Sourjik and Berg, 2004; Studdert and Parkinson, 2004; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ames et al., 2002; Briegel et al., 2012; Sourjik and Berg, 2004; Studdert and Parkinson, 2004; and Zhang et al., 2007.

claim: The coupling of neighboring receptors within clusters allows integration of signals perceived by different types of receptors.
source: The coupling of neighboring receptors within clusters also allows integration of signals perceived by different types of receptors, so that the net response of a cooperative signaling unit is determined by the net of the free-energy changes due to stimulation of individual receptors (Keymer et al., 2006; Mello and Tu, 2005; Neumann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Keymer et al., 2006; Mello and Tu, 2005; and Neumann et al., 2010.

claim: The net response of a cooperative signaling unit is determined by the net of the free-energy changes due to stimulation of individual receptors.
source: The coupling of neighboring receptors within clusters also allows integration of signals perceived by different types of receptors, so that the net response of a cooperative signaling unit is determined by the net of the free-energy changes due to stimulation of individual receptors (Keymer et al., 2006; Mello and Tu, 2005; Neumann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Keymer et al., 2006; Mello and Tu, 2005; and Neumann et al., 2010.

claim: Although the activities of different receptors are tightly coupled, adaptation to stimuli results in preferential methylation of the stimulus-specific receptor.
source: Notably, although the activities of different receptors are tightly coupled, adaptation to stimuli results in preferential methylation of the stimulus-specific receptor (Lan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lan et al., 2011.

claim: Chemotaxis is typically assumed to enable bacteria to find conditions that are optimal for growth.
source: Chemotaxis is typically assumed to enable bacteria to find conditions that are optimal for growth, and correlation between chemotactic and metabolic preferences has indeed been observed for E. coli (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: Correlation between chemotactic and metabolic preferences has been observed for E. coli.
source: Chemotaxis is typically assumed to enable bacteria to find conditions that are optimal for growth, and correlation between chemotactic and metabolic preferences has indeed been observed for E. coli (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: E. coli's response to chemical ligands is usually unidirectional.
source: Consistent with that, E. coli's response to chemical ligands is usually unidirectional, that is cells either follow gradients only upwards (attractant) or only downwards (repellent).
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli chemotaxis.

claim: Gradients of pH, osmolarity, or temperature might need to be followed bidirectionally in order to find optimal growth conditions.
source: In contrast, gradients of other stimuli that are sensed by the chemotaxis pathway, such as pH (Yang and Sourjik, 2012), osmolarity (Adler et al., 1988), or temperature (Maeda et al., 1976), might need to be followed bidirectionally in order to find optimal growth conditions.
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by citations to Yang and Sourjik, 2012; Adler et al., 1988; and Maeda et al., 1976.

claim: The unidirectional chemotactic response of E. coli is comparatively well understood.
source: However, while the unidirectional chemotactic response of E. coli is comparatively well understood, mechanisms of bidirectional taxis in bacteria remain to be established.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Mechanisms of bidirectional taxis in bacteria remain to be established.
source: However, while the unidirectional chemotactic response of E. coli is comparatively well understood, mechanisms of bidirectional taxis in bacteria remain to be established.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: E. coli is well known to follow temperature gradients and to react to temporal changes in temperature, similar to the tactic response to chemical effectors.
source: E. coli is well known to follow temperature gradients and to react to temporal changes in temperature, similar to the tactic response to chemical effectors (Maeda et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maeda et al., 1976.

claim: The tactic response to temperature is mainly mediated by Tar and Tsr.
source: This tactic response to temperature is mainly mediated by Tar and Tsr (Imae et al., 1984; Lee et al., 1988; Maeda and Imae, 1979; Mizuno and Imae, 1984), although minor receptors Trg, Aer, and Tap might also be temperature-sensitive (Nara et al., 1991; Nishiyama et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Imae et al., 1984; Lee et al., 1988; Maeda and Imae, 1979; and Mizuno and Imae, 1984.

claim: Minor receptors Trg, Aer, and Tap might also be temperature-sensitive.
source: This tactic response to temperature is mainly mediated by Tar and Tsr (Imae et al., 1984; Lee et al., 1988; Maeda and Imae, 1979; Mizuno and Imae, 1984), although minor receptors Trg, Aer, and Tap might also be temperature-sensitive (Nara et al., 1991; Nishiyama et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nara et al., 1991 and Nishiyama et al., 2010.

claim: The thermotactic behavior of E. coli is primarily determined by the interplay of the responses mediated by Tar and Tsr.
source: The thermotactic behavior of E. coli is thus primarily determined by the interplay of the responses mediated by Tar and Tsr (Yoney and Salman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoney and Salman, 2015.

claim: At low temperatures, E. coli is normally thermophilic (heat-seeking), with an increase in temperature causing an attractant-like response.
source: At low temperatures, E. coli is normally thermophilic (heat-seeking), with an increase in temperature causing an attractant-like response (Maeda et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maeda et al., 1976.

claim: The thermotactic response of E. coli to higher temperatures (36°C to 42°C) remained ambiguous, with different studies showing either loss of response or its inversion to cryophilic.
source: However, the thermotactic response of E. coli to higher temperatures, 36°C to 42°C, remained ambiguous, with different studies showing either loss of response or its inversion to cryophilic (Maeda et al., 1976; Paster and Ryu, 2008; Yoney and Salman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maeda et al., 1976; Paster and Ryu, 2008; and Yoney and Salman, 2015.

claim: Adaptation to a combination of attractants sensed by Tsr (serine) and Tar (aspartate or MeAsp) can invert the thermotactic response.
source: Adaptation to a combination of attractants sensed by Tsr (serine) and Tar (aspartate or its non-metabolizable analogue α-methyl-DL-aspartate, MeAsp) can clearly invert the thermotactic response (Imae et al., 1984; Salman and Libchaber, 2007), which is likely due to increased methylation of adapted receptors since amino acid replacement of methylation sites also altered thermotactic responses of Tar and Tsr (Nara et al., 1996; Nishiyama et al., 1999a; Nishiyama et al., 1999b; Oleksiuk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Imae et al., 1984 and Salman and Libchaber, 2007.

claim: The inversion of thermotactic response is likely due to increased methylation of adapted receptors.
source: Adaptation to a combination of attractants sensed by Tsr (serine) and Tar (aspartate or its non-metabolizable analogue α-methyl-DL-aspartate, MeAsp) can clearly invert the thermotactic response (Imae et al., 1984; Salman and Libchaber, 2007), which is likely due to increased methylation of adapted receptors since amino acid replacement of methylation sites also altered thermotactic responses of Tar and Tsr (Nara et al., 1996; Nishiyama et al., 1999a; Nishiyama et al., 1999b; Oleksiuk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nara et al., 1996; Nishiyama et al., 1999a; Nishiyama et al., 1999b; and Oleksiuk et al., 2011.

claim: Amino acid replacement of methylation sites altered thermotactic responses of Tar and Tsr.
source: Adaptation to a combination of attractants sensed by Tsr (serine) and Tar (aspartate or its non-metabolizable analogue α-methyl-DL-aspartate, MeAsp) can clearly invert the thermotactic response (Imae et al., 1984; Salman and Libchaber, 2007), which is likely due to increased methylation of adapted receptors since amino acid replacement of methylation sites also altered thermotactic responses of Tar and Tsr (Nara et al., 1996; Nishiyama et al., 1999a; Nishiyama et al., 1999b; Oleksiuk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nara et al., 1996; Nishiyama et al., 1999a; Nishiyama et al., 1999b; and Oleksiuk et al., 2011.

claim: Several studies showed that Tar functions as a warm sensor in low methylation states but as a cold sensor in high methylation states.
source: Several studies showed that Tar functions as a warm sensor in low methylation states but as a cold sensor in high methylation states, whereas Tsr was suggested to similarly function as a warm sensor in low methylation states but to lose its temperature sensitivity in high methylation states (Imae et al., 1984; Salman and Libchaber, 2007; Yoney and Salman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Imae et al., 1984; Salman and Libchaber, 2007; and Yoney and Salman, 2015.

claim: Tsr was suggested to function as a warm sensor in low methylation states but to lose its temperature sensitivity in high methylation states.
source: Several studies showed that Tar functions as a warm sensor in low methylation states but as a cold sensor in high methylation states, whereas Tsr was suggested to similarly function as a warm sensor in low methylation states but to lose its temperature sensitivity in high methylation states (Imae et al., 1984; Salman and Libchaber, 2007; Yoney and Salman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Imae et al., 1984; Salman and Libchaber, 2007; and Yoney and Salman, 2015.

claim: Other work showed that both Tar and Tsr mediate thermophilic response in low-modification states and cryophilic response in high-modification states.
source: In contrast, other work showed that both receptors mediate thermophilic response in the low-modification states (zero or one methyl groups per receptor monomer) and cryophilic response in the high-modification states (Oleksiuk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oleksiuk et al., 2011.

claim: The interpretation of E. coli behavior in gradients of temperature is complicated by the fact that temperature affects cell swimming, respiration, and metabolism.
source: Despite this clear evidence that the thermotactic behavior of E. coli depends on both the ambient temperature and chemotactic stimuli, the interpretation of E. coli behavior in gradients of temperature is complicated by the fact that, besides the signaling pathway, temperature also affects cell swimming, respiration, and metabolism (Demir et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 1976; Salman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Demir et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 1976; and Salman et al., 2006.

claim: The key questions whether E. coli is capable of accumulation at a specific intermediate temperature solely by means of thermotaxis, and the mechanism of such accumulation, remain unanswered.
source: Hence, the key questions whether E. coli is capable of accumulation at a specific intermediate temperature solely by means of thermotaxis, and the mechanism of such accumulation, remain unanswered.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A standard mathematical model of the chemotactic network cannot explain the accumulation temperature.
source: Importantly, a standard mathematical model of the chemotactic network, developed by Barkai and Leibler (Barkai and Leibler, 1997), and generalized to allow for coupled teams of receptors (Keymer et al., 2006; Mello and Tu, 2005; Sourjik and Berg, 2004), cannot explain the accumulation temperature.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the limitations of existing models, supported by citations.

claim: A model that can account for bidirectional taxis (termed 'precision sensing') was proposed.
source: Although a model that can account for the bidirectional taxis (termed 'precision sensing') was proposed (Jiang et al., 2009), this model critically relies on an ad hoc assumption about the temperature dependence of the pathway activity that was not experimentally verified.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2009.

claim: The precision sensing model critically relies on an ad hoc assumption about the temperature dependence of the pathway activity that was not experimentally verified.
source: Although a model that can account for the bidirectional taxis (termed 'precision sensing') was proposed (Jiang et al., 2009), this model critically relies on an ad hoc assumption about the temperature dependence of the pathway activity that was not experimentally verified.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the Jiang et al., 2009 model.

claim: The FRET assay relies on phosphorylation-dependent interactions between CheY and CheZ, which are fused to yellow and cyan fluorescent proteins, respectively.
source: The FRET assay relies on phosphorylation-dependent interactions between CheY and CheZ, which are fused to yellow and cyan fluorescent proteins, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: The formation of the CheY-YFP/CheZ-CFP complex is proportional to the kinase activity of CheA.
source: The formation of the CheY-YFP/CheZ-CFP complex, which is proportional to the kinase activity of CheA, leads to an increase in the ratio of YFP to CFP fluorescence due to energy transfer from CFP to YFP.
evidence: This describes the principle of the FRET assay.

claim: A strain deleted for flgM was used to facilitate FRET measurements.
source: Note that to facilitate the measurements we used a strain deleted for flgM, the negative regulator of flagellar and chemotaxis gene expression, that elevates in proper proportion the levels of chemotaxis proteins and thereby enhances the chemotactic response (Kollmann et al., 2005; Steuer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kollmann et al., 2005 and Steuer et al., 2011.

claim: The response to an increase in temperature revealed a rapid transient decrease of the YFP/CFP ratio, reflecting a decrease in the kinase activity (thermophilic response).
source: Similar to the response observed upon stimulation with a chemical attractant in the same setup (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), the FRET response to an increase in temperature revealed a rapid transient decrease of the YFP/CFP ratio, reflecting a decrease in the kinase activity, that is a thermophilic response (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The transient FRET response to temperature was specific because it was not observed in a ΔcheA strain.
source: This transient response was specific because it was not observed in a ΔcheA strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A decrease in temperature resulted in an opposite response, that is, a transient increase in FRET.
source: A decrease in temperature resulted in an opposite response, that is, a transient increase in FRET, similar to the removal of attractant (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) or the addition of repellent.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The time course of subsequent adaptation in the presence of persistent temperature stimulation was similar for thermal and chemical stimuli.
source: The time course of subsequent adaptation in the presence of persistent stimulation was also similar for thermal and chemical stimuli, indicating that the adaptation to temperature similarly relies on the CheR/CheB receptor methylation system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of adaptation time courses.

claim: Adaptation to temperature relies on the CheR/CheB receptor methylation system.
source: The time course of subsequent adaptation in the presence of persistent stimulation was also similar for thermal and chemical stimuli, indicating that the adaptation to temperature similarly relies on the CheR/CheB receptor methylation system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of adaptation time courses and is directly confirmed by methylation measurements.

claim: The methylation profile of Tsr and Tar shifted towards higher-methylated states at higher temperature.
source: This was directly confirmed by measuring the methylation profile of Tsr and Tar, both of which shifted towards higher-methylated states at higher temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The major noticeable difference between thermal and chemical stimulation in the FRET experiments was an increase in the basal YFP/CFP ratio at higher temperature.
source: The only major noticeable difference between thermal and chemical stimulation in the FRET experiments was an increase in the basal YFP/CFP ratio at higher temperature, which was also seen in the ΔcheA strain and is caused by temperature dependence of YFP and CFP fluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) (Kumar and Sourjik, 2012; Oleksiuk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and citations to Kumar and Sourjik, 2012 and Oleksiuk et al., 2011.

claim: The increase in basal YFP/CFP ratio at higher temperature is caused by temperature dependence of YFP and CFP fluorescence.
source: The only major noticeable difference between thermal and chemical stimulation in the FRET experiments was an increase in the basal YFP/CFP ratio at higher temperature, which was also seen in the ΔcheA strain and is caused by temperature dependence of YFP and CFP fluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) (Kumar and Sourjik, 2012; Oleksiuk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and citations to Kumar and Sourjik, 2012 and Oleksiuk et al., 2011.

claim: The thermophilic response of wild-type cells persisted at a similar level up to 30°C.
source: We observed that the thermophilic response of wild-type cells persisted at a similar level up to 30°C, but decreased rapidly at higher ambient temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The thermophilic response decreased rapidly at ambient temperatures higher than 30°C.
source: We observed that the thermophilic response of wild-type cells persisted at a similar level up to 30°C, but decreased rapidly at higher ambient temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Even at the highest tested temperature (jump from 39°C to 42°C), the response remained weakly thermophilic.
source: Nevertheless, even at the highest tested temperature (jump from 39°C to 42°C), the response remained weakly thermophilic.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: For cells adapted in buffer, no inversion of the pathway response to temperature was observed.
source: Hence, for cells that were adapted in the buffer (in the absence of chemoattractants) we did not observe any inversion of the pathway response to temperature.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The FRET results were generally consistent with the behavioral response of motile cells in a thermal gradient established across a microfluidic channel.
source: These results were generally consistent with the behavioral response of motile cells in a thermal gradient established across a microfluidic channel (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: When adapted in buffer, cells accumulated towards the warmer side of the gradient in the microfluidic channel, consistent with thermophilic behavior.
source: Here, when adapted in the buffer, cells accumulated towards the warmer side of the gradient in the channel, consistent with thermophilic behavior (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The thermophilic behavior weakened in the range of higher temperatures but never inverted in microfluidics assays.
source: In line with the FRET-based pathway-activity analysis, this thermophilic behavior weakened in the range of higher temperatures but never inverted.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Both FRET and microfluidics assays show that in the absence of chemotactic stimuli, E. coli has an exclusively thermophilic response that decreases at high ambient temperatures.
source: Thus, the results of both FRET and microfluidics assays clearly show that in the absence of chemotactic stimuli, E. coli has an exclusively thermophilic response that decreases at high ambient temperatures, but it does not actively avoid high temperature.
evidence: This is supported by data from both FRET (Figure 1B) and microfluidics (Figure 1C) experiments.

claim: E. coli does not actively avoid high temperature in the absence of chemotactic stimuli.
source: Thus, the results of both FRET and microfluidics assays clearly show that in the absence of chemotactic stimuli, E. coli has an exclusively thermophilic response that decreases at high ambient temperatures, but it does not actively avoid high temperature.
evidence: This is supported by data from both FRET (Figure 1B) and microfluidics (Figure 1C) experiments.

claim: Steady pre-stimulation with high levels of both MeAsp and serine inverted the response to cryophilic over the entire range of temperatures.
source: Indeed, steady pre-stimulation with high levels of both attractants inverted the response to cryophilic over the entire range of temperatures, with the response again becoming weaker at high temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At low concentrations of attractants the response remained thermophilic and no avoidance of high temperature was observed.
source: At low concentrations of attractants the response remained thermophilic and no avoidance of high temperature was observed but the response amplitude was reduced compared to buffer-adapted cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Adaptation to intermediate levels of serine and MeAsp completely abolished the thermotactic response over the entire range of tested temperatures.
source: Adaptation to intermediate levels of serine and MeAsp completely abolished the thermotactic response over the entire range of tested temperatures, meaning that the pathway becomes temperature-insensitive when both major chemoreceptors are stimulated at an approximately equal intermediate level.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The pathway becomes temperature-insensitive when both major chemoreceptors are stimulated at an approximately equal intermediate level.
source: Adaptation to intermediate levels of serine and MeAsp completely abolished the thermotactic response over the entire range of tested temperatures, meaning that the pathway becomes temperature-insensitive when both major chemoreceptors are stimulated at an approximately equal intermediate level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Adaptation to MeAsp or serine alone had nearly identical effect on the thermotactic response.
source: In contrast to previous reports (Imae et al., 1984; Salman and Libchaber, 2007; Yoney and Salman, 2015), we observed that adaptation to MeAsp (Figure 2B) or serine (Figure 2C) had nearly identical effect on the thermotactic response.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2C.

claim: Adaptation to either MeAsp or serine weakened the thermophilic response in a dose-dependent manner and could eventually invert it to cryophilic.
source: As in the case of stimulation with a mixture of serine and MeAsp, we observed that adaptation to either attractant weakened the thermophilic response in a dose-dependent manner and could eventually invert it to cryophilic.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2C.

claim: The pattern of response inversion by individual attractants was clearly different from combined stimulation.
source: However, the pattern of this inversion by individual attractants was clearly different.
evidence: This is supported by comparing data in Figure 2A with Figure 2B and Figure 2C.

claim: Cells adapted to individual attractants showed cryophilic response at high temperature but retained thermophilic response at low temperatures.
source: Whereas combined stimulation either inverted or abolished the thermotactic response over the entire temperature range (Figure 2A), cells adapted to individual attractants showed cryophilic response at high temperature but retained thermophilic response at low temperatures (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2C.

claim: An inversion ('cross-over') temperature, where the FRET response changes from thermophilic to cryophilic, implies that E. coli can bidirectionally accumulate towards a preferred temperature using the chemotaxis pathway.
source: Such an inversion ('cross-over') temperature, where the FRET response changes from thermophilic to cryophilic, implies that E. coli can indeed bidirectionally accumulate towards a preferred temperature using the chemotaxis pathway.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2C.

claim: The inversion and accumulation temperatures may not be exactly identical due to weak direct effects of temperature on E. coli motility.
source: However, the inversion and accumulation temperatures may not be exactly identical due to weak direct effects of temperature on E. coli motility (Oleksiuk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oleksiuk et al., 2011.

claim: A combination of serine and MeAsp changed the response to cryophilic in microfluidic experiments.
source: These conclusions were confirmed by microfluidic experiments, where a combination of serine and MeAsp changed the response to cryophilic (Figure 2D) and where, in the presence of individual attractants, the response turned from thermophilic at low temperatures to cryophilic at high temperatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the presence of individual attractants, the response turned from thermophilic at low temperatures to cryophilic at high temperatures in microfluidic experiments.
source: These conclusions were confirmed by microfluidic experiments, where a combination of serine and MeAsp changed the response to cryophilic (Figure 2D) and where, in the presence of individual attractants, the response turned from thermophilic at low temperatures to cryophilic at high temperatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In a thermal gradient and in presence of either one of the major chemoattractants cells should accumulate at some transition temperature.
source: This latter inversion of the thermotactic response dependent on the ambient temperature implies that in a thermal gradient and in presence of either one of the major chemoattractants cells should accumulate at some transition temperature (which is expected to be close to the inversion temperature in the FRET assay), being attracted to it from both lower and higher temperatures.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the observed response inversion.

claim: Cell accumulation at a transition temperature was observed in the presence of serine in a gradient that spanned a range of temperatures with both thermophilic and cryophilic responses.
source: Such accumulation was indeed observed in the presence of serine in a gradient that spanned a range of temperatures with both thermophilic and cryophilic responses (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: No cell accumulation was observed in the same thermal gradient in the absence of attractant stimulation.
source: Notably, no cell accumulation was observed in the same thermal gradient in the absence of attractant stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), meaning that it is not simply due to the wider temperature range used in these experiments.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Chemotactic stimulation of Tar or Tsr individually – but not together – creates an accumulation temperature.
source: Our observation that chemotactic stimulation of Tar or Tsr individually – but not together – creates an accumulation temperature indicates that the effect might be related to the interplay between the two receptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: In the absence of chemoattractants both Tar- and Tsr-only cells exhibited thermophilic responses that decreased with ambient temperature.
source: Similar to wild-type cells, in the absence of chemoattractants both Tar- and Tsr-only cells exhibited thermophilic responses that decreased with ambient temperature.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B.

claim: Adaptation to their respective attractants decreased and inverted the thermophilic response in a dose-dependent manner for both Tar-only and Tsr-only cells.
source: Adaptation to their respective attractants also decreased and inverted the thermophilic response in a dose-dependent manner, which was again similar for both receptors.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B.

claim: The inversion to cryophilic response in Tar-only and Tsr-only cells occurred over the entire temperature range at any given concentration of serine or MeAsp.
source: Notably, the inversion to cryophilic response occurred over the entire temperature range and no significant cross-over from thermophilic to cryophilic response occurred with the change of temperature at any given concentration of serine or MeAsp.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B.

claim: The responses of the Tar and Tsr-only cells were similar to the response of wild-type cells adapted to combinations of serine and MeAsp.
source: The responses of the Tar and Tsr-only cells were thus similar to the response of wild-type cells adapted to combinations of serine and MeAsp (Figure 2A), but different from adaptation to only one of these chemoattractants (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figure 3A,B with Figure 2A,B,C.

claim: Chemotactic stimulation of Tar or Tsr can either inhibit or invert their thermosensing properties.
source: These observations confirm that chemotactic stimulation of Tar or Tsr can either inhibit or invert their thermosensing properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B.

claim: In the presence of only one receptor type there is no temperature-dependent response inversion at any given level of chemotactic stimulation, and thus no accumulation temperature.
source: The results also clearly demonstrate that in the presence of only one receptor type there is no temperature-dependent response inversion at any given level of chemotactic stimulation, and thus no accumulation temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B.

claim: The observed dependence of the thermotactic response on ambient temperature and chemotactic stimulation is likely to be explained by the known effects of methylation on receptor thermosensing.
source: The observed dependence of the thermotactic response on ambient temperature and chemotactic stimulation is likely to be explained by the known effects of methylation on receptor thermosensing (Imae et al., 1984; Nara et al., 1996; Nishiyama et al., 1997; Paster and Ryu, 2008; Salman and Libchaber, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The results are consistent with a previous observation suggesting that the interplay between methylation and thermosensing is similar for Tar and Tsr.
source: Our results are consistent with a previous observation suggesting that the interplay between methylation and thermosensing is similar for Tar and Tsr (Oleksiuk et al., 2011), which both mediate thermophilic response in low-methylation states but cryophilic response in high-methylation states.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oleksiuk et al., 2011.

claim: Tar and Tsr both mediate thermophilic response in low-methylation states but cryophilic response in high-methylation states.
source: Our results are consistent with a previous observation suggesting that the interplay between methylation and thermosensing is similar for Tar and Tsr (Oleksiuk et al., 2011), which both mediate thermophilic response in low-methylation states but cryophilic response in high-methylation states.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oleksiuk et al., 2011 and by data in the current study.

claim: For buffer adapted cells, where the level of receptor modification is low, the response of both receptors is thermophilic.
source: For the buffer adapted cells, where the level of receptor modification is low (Endres et al., 2008), the response of both receptors is thus thermophilic.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Endres et al., 2008 and by data in the current study.

claim: Adaptation to positive (attractant-like) temperature stimuli is mediated by increased methylation of receptors.
source: However, because adaptation to positive (attractant-like) temperature stimuli is mediated by increased methylation of receptors (Figure 3C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the thermophilic response becomes weaker at higher temperature.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For cells of single-receptor strains adapted at high concentration of the respective chemoattractant, the methylation level is high and the response is cryophilic.
source: In contrast, for cells of single-receptor strains adapted at high concentration of the respective chemoattractant, the methylation level is high and the response is thus cryophilic.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 3B, and Figure 3C.

claim: Adaptation to cryophilic response leads to increased demethylation of receptors at higher temperature.
source: Adaptation to this repellent-like response leads to increased demethylation of receptors at higher temperature (Figure 3C), thus weakening the cryophilic response.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At intermediate levels of chemotactic stimulation that correspond to zero thermotactic response, there are no associated changes in receptor methylation and therefore no switch from thermophilic to cryophilic behavior.
source: At intermediate levels of chemotactic stimulation that correspond to zero thermotactic response, there are no associated changes in receptor methylation and therefore no switch from thermophilic to cryophilic behavior.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of adaptation.

claim: Glycine has much lower apparent affinity to Tsr compared to serine.
source: This discrepancy can be explained by the much lower apparent affinity of glycine to Tsr compared to serine (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: At glycine concentrations of up to 1 mM, the temperature response of the Tsr-only strain is either thermophilic or non-detectable.
source: Indeed, in FRET experiments we found that at glycine concentrations of up to 1 mM, the temperature response of the Tsr-only strain is either thermophilic or non-detectable (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The response of the Tsr-only strain became weakly cryophilic only when the concentration of glycine was increased to 30 mM.
source: The response of the Tsr-only strain became weakly cryophilic only when the concentration of glycine was increased to a very high level of 30 mM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Prolonged incubation of bacterial culture in complex medium resulted in substantial depletion of serine from the medium.
source: Notably, in these experiments the exposure of bacterial culture to a thermal gradient was preceded by a prolonged incubation, which most likely resulted in substantial depletion of serine from the medium as it is rapidly consumed by E. coli (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015 and by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Serine is rapidly consumed by E. coli.
source: Notably, in these experiments the exposure of bacterial culture to a thermal gradient was preceded by a prolonged incubation, which most likely resulted in substantial depletion of serine from the medium as it is rapidly consumed by E. coli (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: Serine depletion from M9CG medium could be confirmed.
source: Such depletion could indeed be confirmed (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary material), suggesting that during the thermotaxis assays, cells were primarily stimulated by only one major chemoattractant, aspartate.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: An accumulation temperature arises from the interplay between Tar and Tsr when only one type is strongly stimulated by its ligand.
source: Our results strongly suggest that an accumulation temperature arises from the interplay between Tar and Tsr when only one type is strongly stimulated by its ligand.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The level of chemotactic stimulation that leads to the response inversion as well as the accumulation temperature might be affected by the relative expression levels of Tar and Tsr.
source: This suggests that the level of chemotactic stimulation that leads to the response inversion as well as the accumulation temperature might be affected by the relative expression levels of Tar and Tsr.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the interplay between the two receptors.

claim: The relative expression levels of Tar and Tsr vary with the growth phase of an E. coli culture, with Tsr being more abundant during the early to mid-exponential phase.
source: Because these levels are known to vary with the growth phase of an E. coli culture, with Tsr being more abundant during the early to mid-exponential phase (Kalinin et al., 2010; Yang and Sourjik, 2012), we tested the thermotactic response in cultures grown to different optical densities (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kalinin et al., 2010 and Yang and Sourjik, 2012.

claim: Cells adapted to high concentrations of serine showed earlier response inversion when grown to low optical density.
source: Indeed, we observed that cells adapted to high concentrations of serine showed earlier response inversion (i.e., inverted at lower temperature) when grown to low optical density, and did not invert at all when grown to high optical density.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cells adapted to high concentrations of serine did not invert at all when grown to high optical density.
source: Indeed, we observed that cells adapted to high concentrations of serine showed earlier response inversion (i.e., inverted at lower temperature) when grown to low optical density, and did not invert at all when grown to high optical density.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The opposite dependence on the growth phase was observed for MeAsp-stimulated cells, which inverted at higher temperature when grown to low optical density.
source: The opposite dependence on the growth phase was observed for MeAsp-stimulated cells, which inverted at higher temperature when grown to low optical density.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The low abundance of Trg, Aer, and Tap as compared to Tar and Tsr makes it unlikely that they significantly contribute to the thermotactic response of wild-type cells.
source: While other receptors might also be temperature sensitive (Nara et al., 1991; Nishiyama et al., 2010), their low abundance in E. coli as compared to the abundances of Tar and Tsr (Li and Hazelbauer, 2004) makes it unlikely that they significantly contribute to the thermotactic response of wild-type cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nara et al., 1991; Nishiyama et al., 2010; and Li and Hazelbauer, 2004.

claim: Adaptation to the ligands of Trg (glucose, galactose) or Tap (dipeptides) had no noticeable effect on the thermotactic response.
source: Indeed, adaptation to the ligands of Trg (glucose, galactose) or Tap (dipeptides) had no noticeable effect on the thermotactic response (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The standard model of the chemotactic network cannot explain the observed accumulation of E. coli towards a specific temperature when both Tsr and Tar receptors are present with one type stimulated by attractant.
source: As mentioned above, the standard model of the chemotactic network cannot explain the observed accumulation of E. coli towards a specific temperature when both Tsr and Tar receptors are present with one type stimulated by attractant.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing models.

claim: The mathematical model incorporates the failure of precise adaptation when the number of available methylation or demethylation sites becomes small.
source: Importantly, this model incorporates the failure of precise adaptation when the number of available methylation or demethylation sites becomes small (Meir et al., 2010), which we believe is essential to explain the accumulation temperature.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meir et al., 2010.

claim: The model captures correctly the complete inversion of the thermal response from thermophilic to cryophilic with methylation level or ligand concentration for a single type of receptor.
source: As clear from the comparison of the data (Figure 2B,C and Figure 3A) to the results of the mathematical model, the model captures correctly the complete inversion of the thermal response form thermophilic to cryophilic with methylation level or ligand concentration (Figure 4A) for a single type of receptor, as well as cross-over (i.e., temperature-dependent inversion) of the response for mixed receptors (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 2B,C and Figure 3A with model results in Figure 4A.

claim: The model captures correctly the cross-over (temperature-dependent inversion) of the response for mixed receptors.
source: As clear from the comparison of the data (Figure 2B,C and Figure 3A) to the results of the mathematical model, the model captures correctly the complete inversion of the thermal response form thermophilic to cryophilic with methylation level or ligand concentration (Figure 4A) for a single type of receptor, as well as cross-over (i.e., temperature-dependent inversion) of the response for mixed receptors (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data with model results in Figure 4B.

claim: For a single receptor type, changes of temperature alone can never change the sign of the thermal response.
source: Changes of temperature alone can never change the sign of the thermal response because if the thermal response approaches zero, as necessary for a sign change, so necessarily does the adaptive change in methylation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the model.

claim: An inversion of the response at a certain temperature becomes possible if changes of temperature lead to a net change in receptor methylation.
source: However, an inversion of the response at a certain temperature becomes possible if changes of temperature lead to a net change in receptor methylation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the model.

claim: When receptors of one type are near the saturation level of their methylation, they cannot adapt perfectly.
source: This is exactly what happens in our mathematical model: when receptors of one type are near the saturation level of their methylation, they cannot adapt perfectly, that is their methylation level changes only weakly upon temperature stimulation, and thus cannot compensate for the response of receptor of the other type, which undergo an opposite and larger change in their methylation level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by model results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The resulting net change in total methylation of the receptor system can produce a change in the sign of the overall thermal response, leading to an inversion of the response at a certain temperature.
source: The resulting net change in total methylation of the receptor system can readily produce a change in the sign of the overall thermal response, leading to an inversion of the response at a certain temperature.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the model.

claim: The actual value of the inversion temperature depends on receptor methylation levels and is thus a function of attractant concentrations.
source: The actual value of the inversion temperature depends on receptor methylation levels and is thus a function of attractant concentrations.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the model.

claim: The model for the inversion temperature relies on the slowing of methylation rates near saturation previously introduced to explain the failure of precise adaptation in chemotaxis.
source: Note that our model for the inversion temperature relies on exactly the same slowing of methylation rates near saturation previously introduced to explain the failure of precise adaptation in chemotaxis (Meir et al., 2010), and it requires no further ad-hoc assumptions about differences between thermosensing properties of Tar and Tsr or asymmetry between thermophilic and cryophilic responses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meir et al., 2010.

claim: The model requires no ad-hoc assumptions about differences between thermosensing properties of Tar and Tsr or asymmetry between thermophilic and cryophilic responses.
source: Note that our model for the inversion temperature relies on exactly the same slowing of methylation rates near saturation previously introduced to explain the failure of precise adaptation in chemotaxis (Meir et al., 2010), and it requires no further ad-hoc assumptions about differences between thermosensing properties of Tar and Tsr or asymmetry between thermophilic and cryophilic responses.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's assumptions.

claim: The model of Jiang et al. attributes an accumulation temperature to temperature-dependent adapted activity.
source: This contrasts with the model of Jiang et al. (Jiang et al., 2009), which attributes an accumulation temperature to temperature-dependent adapted activity, but which does not explain why an inversion temperature only occurs when both Tar and Tsr are present and then in the presence of ligand for only one of the two receptor types.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2009.

claim: The model of Jiang et al. does not explain why an inversion temperature only occurs when both Tar and Tsr are present and then in the presence of ligand for only one of the two receptor types.
source: This contrasts with the model of Jiang et al. (Jiang et al., 2009), which attributes an accumulation temperature to temperature-dependent adapted activity, but which does not explain why an inversion temperature only occurs when both Tar and Tsr are present and then in the presence of ligand for only one of the two receptor types.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the Jiang et al., 2009 model.

claim: The effect of serine on E. coli growth was temperature-dependent.
source: We thus investigated this toxicity of serine for E. coli MG1655 in M9 glycerol minimal medium as a function of growth temperature. We observed that the effect of serine on E. coli growth was indeed temperature-dependent: whereas at low temperature (24°C) serine is growth-promoting (Figure 5A), it becomes inhibitory at high temperature (39°C) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5B.

claim: At low temperature (24°C) serine is growth-promoting.
source: We observed that the effect of serine on E. coli growth was indeed temperature-dependent: whereas at low temperature (24°C) serine is growth-promoting (Figure 5A), it becomes inhibitory at high temperature (39°C) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Serine becomes inhibitory at high temperature (39°C).
source: We observed that the effect of serine on E. coli growth was indeed temperature-dependent: whereas at low temperature (24°C) serine is growth-promoting (Figure 5A), it becomes inhibitory at high temperature (39°C) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The observed delay in growth in the presence of serine was minimal at 30°C.
source: Interestingly, the observed delay in growth in the presence of serine was minimal at 30°C (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The effect of aspartate on growth was much weaker than serine.
source: By comparison, the effect of aspartate on growth was much weaker.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: For cells adapted in the presence of serine, the emergence of an accumulation temperature might be an adaptive mechanism that enables E. coli to optimize its growth.
source: These results indicate that at least for cells adapted in the presence of serine, the emergence of an accumulation temperature might have a simple physiological meaning, being an adaptive mechanism that enables E. coli to optimize its growth in the presence of this amino acid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the growth data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The entire complexity of the thermotactic behavior of E. coli can be accounted for by the interplay between the effects of temperature on the activity of the major chemoreceptors Tar and Tsr and the dependence of receptor methylation on both ambient temperature and chemoeffector stimulation.
source: Our results show that the entire complexity of the thermotactic behavior of E. coli can be accounted for by the interplay between the effects of temperature on the activity of the major chemoreceptors Tar and Tsr and the dependence of receptor methylation on both ambient temperature and chemoeffector stimulation
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data and modeling.

claim: The symmetric regulation of the thermal response for Tar and Tsr is in contrast to previous studies that suggested that only Tar can function both as a warm and cold sensor with Tsr acting either as a warm sensor or not responding.
source: Such symmetric regulation of the thermal response for Tar and Tsr is in contrast to previous studies that suggested that only Tar can function both as a warm and cold sensor with Tsr acting either as a warm sensor or not responding (Imae et al., 1984; Salman and Libchaber, 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies, supported by citations to Imae et al., 1984 and Salman and Libchaber, 2007.

claim: The cryophilic response observed at high levels of ligand stimulation shows less dependence on ambient temperature than the thermophilic response.
source: Notably, the cryophilic response observed at high levels of ligand stimulation shows less dependence on ambient temperature than the thermophilic response.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data.

claim: Upon adaptation to either one of Tar or Tsr ligands, only the cognate receptor is preferentially methylated and thus inverted in its thermosensing.
source: Finally, upon adaptation to either one of Tar or Tsr ligands, only the cognate receptor is preferentially methylated (Lan et al., 2011) and thus inverted in its thermosensing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lan et al., 2011.

claim: In nature E. coli is unlikely to be stimulated by a single amino acid.
source: Although in nature E. coli is unlikely to be stimulated by a single amino acid, the mechanism proposed here applies as long as the concentrations of serine and aspartate in the medium are strongly different.
evidence: This is a speculation about natural conditions.

claim: The mechanism proposed applies as long as the concentrations of serine and aspartate in the medium are strongly different.
source: Although in nature E. coli is unlikely to be stimulated by a single amino acid, the mechanism proposed here applies as long as the concentrations of serine and aspartate in the medium are strongly different.
evidence: This is an inference about the applicability of the mechanism.

claim: E. coli chemotaxis has evolved to primarily follow gradients of individual amino acids rather than of amino acid mixtures.
source: Such a scenario is consistent with a recent study suggesting that E. coli chemotaxis has evolved to primarily follow gradients of individual amino acids rather than of amino acid mixtures (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: The cross-over from thermophilic to cryophilic response relies on the previously characterized failure of precise adaptation in bacterial chemotaxis.
source: Our analysis suggests that the cross-over from thermophilic to cryophilic response relies on the previously characterized failure of precise adaptation in bacterial chemotaxis (Meir et al., 2010; Neumann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meir et al., 2010 and Neumann et al., 2014.

claim: The failure of precise adaptation occurs at high levels of receptor methylation, which lowers the rate of further methylation.
source: This failure occurs at high levels of receptor methylation, which lowers the rate of further methylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about adaptation failure.

claim: The model can naturally explain the apparent difference between the thermophilic and cryophilic responses as a function of ambient temperature.
source: Importantly, our model does not require any ad-hoc assumptions of differences between the thermosensing behavior of Tar and Tsr or of the temperature dependence of other pathway parameters, and it can naturally explain the apparent difference between the thermophilic and cryophilic responses as a function of ambient temperature.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's capabilities.

claim: The inversion of the thermotactic response by individual attractants strongly depends on the ratio between Tar and Tsr.
source: Consistent with this model of the interplay between Tar and Tsr and with previous observations (Yoney and Salman, 2015), we demonstrate that the inversion of the thermotactic response by individual attractants strongly depends on the ratio between these two receptors, which itself is a function of the growth phase of the cell culture (Kalinin et al., 2010; Salman and Libchaber, 2007; Yang and Sourjik, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and citations to Yoney and Salman, 2015; Kalinin et al., 2010; Salman and Libchaber, 2007; and Yang and Sourjik, 2012.

claim: The ratio between Tar and Tsr is a function of the growth phase of the cell culture.
source: Consistent with this model of the interplay between Tar and Tsr and with previous observations (Yoney and Salman, 2015), we demonstrate that the inversion of the thermotactic response by individual attractants strongly depends on the ratio between these two receptors, which itself is a function of the growth phase of the cell culture (Kalinin et al., 2010; Salman and Libchaber, 2007; Yang and Sourjik, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kalinin et al., 2010; Salman and Libchaber, 2007; and Yang and Sourjik, 2012.

claim: Bidirectional thermotaxis requires asymmetric stimulation of either one of the two major receptors, Tar or Tsr.
source: Although largely consistent with previous studies on thermotaxis, including a recent work that emphasized the importance of the interplay between Tar and Tsr (Yoney and Salman, 2015), surprisingly our results demonstrate that bidirectional thermotaxis requires asymmetric stimulation of either one of the two major receptors, Tar or Tsr.
evidence: This is a key conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The differences with previous studies are likely to be explained by the very low signaling strength of glycine.
source: These differences are likely to be explained first by the very low signaling strength of glycine (Yang et al., 2015), the Tsr attractant used in two of these studies (Salman and Libchaber, 2007; Yoney and Salman, 2015), and second by the weaker cryophilic response mediated by Tsr that apparently eluded detection by Mizuno and Imae (Imae et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015 and by data in the current study.

claim: The weaker cryophilic response mediated by Tsr apparently eluded detection by Mizuno and Imae.
source: These differences are likely to be explained first by the very low signaling strength of glycine (Yang et al., 2015), the Tsr attractant used in two of these studies (Salman and Libchaber, 2007; Yoney and Salman, 2015), and second by the weaker cryophilic response mediated by Tsr that apparently eluded detection by Mizuno and Imae (Imae et al., 1984).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous work, supported by citation to Imae et al., 1984.

claim: Secretion of attractants into the medium during long pre-stimulus incubation may explain the inversion of the thermotactic response at high temperature observed by Paster and Ryu.
